options.B: Sample production traffic at random plus the flagged cases, score it with a calibrated judge and periodic human review, combine it with feedback signals, and feed failures to the offline suite.
options.C: Ask the model itself after each answer whether it was correct and record the result.
options.D: Wait until feedback volume rises on its own before measuring.

explanation:
B is right because random sampling removes the self-selection in feedback, a calibrated judge scales review, and failures improve the offline suite.
A fails because the sample is small and biased toward unhappy users.
D fails because waiting leaves quality unmeasured.
C fails because an uncalibrated self-report is not independent evidence.

question: In a retrieval evaluation for a policy assistant, the correct passage appears in the top 50 candidates for 96% of questions but in the top 5 for only 61%. The generation prompt gets the top 5. Where should the team invest first?

options.A: Increase the number of embedding dimensions and re-index the corpus.
options.B: Fine-tune the generation prompt to ignore irrelevant passages among the top 5.
options.C: Pass all 50 candidates to the model to guarantee the passage is included.
options.D: Add a reranking stage that scores the top candidates and passes the best few to the model, then re-measure precision at the top.

explanation:
D is right because recall is good but ranking is poor, which is the problem a reranker addresses.
A fails because the candidate pool already contains the answer, so a bigger embedding does not target ordering.
C fails because it adds cost, latency and distractors, and may degrade accuracy.
B fails because if the right passage is not among the top 5, a prompt cannot use it.

question: An input-screening classifier for a customer chatbot blocks 8% of legitimate requests, and users are complaining, while a red team still finds a few evasions. The security lead wants to tune the guardrail. What is the best way to proceed?

options.A: Measure false positives and false negatives on a labeled set drawn from real traffic and red-team cases, weigh the cost of each error type for this use case, and tune thresholds or add layers accordingly.
options.B: Disable the classifier, since it hurts the experience and other controls exist.
options.C: Tighten the classifier threshold until no attacks pass, ignoring legitimate blocks.
options.D: Loosen it until no complaints arrive, and rely on the system prompt for the rest.

explanation:
A is right because tuning needs measured error rates on representative data and a decision about which error costs more.
C fails because maximal strictness drives false positives up and hurts the product.
B fails because removing the layer without evidence removes protection.
D fails because tuning for silence ignores the evasions, and the prompt is not an enforceable control.

question: An MCP server team renamed a tool parameter and made a new field required. Agents in three downstream products began failing at the first call, and the first signal was customer complaints. How should the team manage this kind of change in future?

options.A: Change tool descriptions to explain the new parameter in more detail so the model adapts.
options.B: Stop changing the server after release, and create a new server for any improvement.
options.C: Announce changes in a channel and expect each team to update their prompts on the day of release.
options.D: Treat schema changes as versioned contracts: make additive and optional changes by default, publish a new version for breaking ones with an overlap and deprecation period, and run consumer contract tests in CI.

explanation:
D is right because tools are an API contract consumed by other systems, so breaking changes need versioning, an overlap period, and automated checks.
C fails because announcements do not prevent breakage or give a safe migration window.
A fails because a clearer description does not make an old client send a field that did not exist.
B fails because freezing servers is impractical and proliferates versions without a migration policy.

question: A research agent browses the web, can read an internal wiki, and can issue HTTP requests, including loading images by URL when it renders a report. A red team plants a web page that instructs the agent to read a confidential wiki page and encode it into an image URL on an attacker's domain. Which control most directly closes this path?

options.A: Switch the agent to a model with a larger context window.
options.B: Log all outbound requests and review them weekly.
options.C: Enforce an egress allowlist at the network and renderer level so that the agent cannot make requests to arbitrary domains, and scope wiki access to what the task needs.
options.D: Add a system prompt warning that web pages may contain malicious instructions.

explanation:
C is right because the attack combines private data, untrusted input and an outbound channel, and a deterministic egress control removes the channel whatever the page says.
D fails because a warning is advisory and the injected text can still win.
B fails because weekly review detects exfiltration after it occurs.
A fails because context size is unrelated to the attack.

question: A legal-research assistant sometimes states confident claims that its retrieved documents do not support. The team wants stronger grounding practices. Which two should they adopt? (Choose two.)

options.A: Require answers to cite the retrieved passages they rely on, and verify that each cited quote exists in the source.
options.B: Allow and encourage the model to state that the evidence is insufficient, and surface a confidence or coverage signal to users when retrieval is weak.
options.C: Set sampling temperature to zero so that the model can only produce true statements.
options.D: Increase chunk size until each retrieved chunk contains the whole document.
options.E: Instruct the model never to say it is unsure, so that users trust the product more.

explanation:
A is right because citations that are mechanically verified make unsupported claims detectable.
B is right because uncertainty declaration and confidence signals let users and systems treat weak evidence differently.
C fails because low temperature reduces variation but does not make claims true.
E fails because forbidding uncertainty encourages fabrication.
D fails because whole-document chunks add noise and cost and still do not force grounding.

question: A supervisor asks a worker agent to 'investigate the checkout outage'. The worker spends several minutes, touches unrelated services, and returns a long narrative that the supervisor cannot use. Which change to the delegation most directly improves results?

options.A: Ask the worker to think step by step before it answers, with no other change to the request.
options.B: Allow the worker to spawn its own sub-workers whenever it finds the task ambiguous.
options.C: Delegate with an explicit goal, constraints and scope, a required output schema, and a stopping condition.
options.D: Give the worker the supervisor's entire conversation history so that it has all the context.

explanation:
C is right because an underspecified delegation produces unfocused work, and a clear contract makes the result usable and bounded.
D fails because dumping the full history adds noise and breaks context isolation.
B fails because more delegation compounds the ambiguity.
A fails because reasoning style does not define scope or output format.

question: A document Q&A feature places the user's name, the date and the session id at the top of the prompt, followed by a 25k-token policy manual that is identical for all users. Cache read tokens are close to zero. Which change best raises the cache hit rate?

options.A: Shorten the manual so that it fits in fewer tokens.
options.B: Make the user name and date identical for all users.
options.C: Put the static manual first and the per-user, per-request values after it, with the cache breakpoint at the end of the static content.
options.D: Add a second copy of the manual at the end of the prompt.

explanation:
C is right because caching works on the exact prefix, so the shared content must come first and the variable content last.
A fails because the cache misses regardless of length when the beginning of the prompt differs for every request.
D fails because duplicating content adds tokens without making the prefix match.
B fails because it breaks the personalization the feature needs.

question: An agent that summarizes build logs sometimes states that all tests passed when some failed. Engineers find that the harness truncates any tool output over 10,000 characters, silently dropping the end, and the failure summary sits at the end of the log. What is the right fix?

options.A: Increase the temperature so that the model explores alternative interpretations.
options.B: Replace the model with one that reads logs more accurately.
options.C: Fix the harness: paginate or summarize large tool outputs, and tell the model explicitly when output was truncated, so that it never treats a partial result as complete.
options.D: Tell the model in the prompt to be cautious when it reports test results.

explanation:
C is right because the defect is in the harness, which hid truncation from the model, so the model was reasoning on incomplete evidence.
D fails because caution cannot recover information the model never saw.
B fails because no model can read text that was dropped.
A fails because randomness does not supply the missing log lines.

question: A team upgraded to a newer Claude model and, in the same release, rewrote the system prompt to take advantage of it. A week later, support tickets show a drop in answer quality for a particular product area. Nobody can tell whether the model or the prompt is responsible. What should the team do now, and in future releases?

options.A: Revert only the model, since models cause most regressions, and keep the new prompt.
options.B: Roll back to the previous known good combination, then evaluate the new model with the old prompt and the new prompt with the old model separately, and release one change at a time.
options.C: Fix the symptom with an additional paragraph in the new prompt addressing that product area.
options.D: Keep both changes and ask the model to self-assess its answers in the affected product area.

explanation:
B is right because attributing a regression needs the variables separated, and a rollback restores service while the experiments run.
D fails because self-assessment is an unvalidated judge and the cause remains unknown.
A fails because it assumes the cause rather than testing it.
C fails because patching the prompt without knowing the cause adds a third change to an unattributed regression.

question: A multi-agent workflow produces a wrong result in about 3% of runs. Engineers cannot reproduce it by running the case once or twice. Which investigation approach is best?

options.A: Replay the captured inputs many times to measure the failure rate, then vary one factor at a time, such as a model, a prompt version or a tool result, to localize the cause.
options.B: Disable parallel execution permanently, since parallelism always causes flaky behavior.
options.C: Rewrite the prompts of all agents with clearer instructions and ship.
options.D: Run the case a couple more times, and if it passes, close the issue as a transient glitch.

explanation:
A is right because non-deterministic failures are properties of rates, and controlled replays with single-variable changes let you test hypotheses.
D fails because a couple of passes cannot rule out a 3% failure.
C fails because it changes many variables without evidence.
B fails because it assumes a cause and gives up throughput.

question: A team is adding backpressure so that a traffic spike does not turn into a retry storm against the Claude API. Which two measures are appropriate? (Choose two.)

options.A: Make the queue unbounded so that no request is ever rejected.
options.B: Retry failed requests immediately, so the queue drains as fast as possible.
options.C: Place a bounded queue in front of the API client and shed or defer low-priority work, returning a clear overload response to callers when the queue is full.
options.D: Admit requests based on estimated token consumption against the remaining capacity, rather than only counting requests.
options.E: Raise client timeouts to several minutes so that queued requests are never abandoned.

explanation:
C is right because a bounded queue with load shedding keeps memory and latency under control and tells callers the truth.
D is right because tokens are the usual binding resource for large prompts.
A fails because an unbounded queue turns a spike into unbounded latency and memory growth.
B fails because immediate retries multiply load.
E fails because long timeouts hold resources and hide the overload.

question: A product manager wants to ship a new prompt because after two days and 600 sessions, thumbs-up rate rose from 71% to 73%, while cost per session rose by 25%. No success metric or sample size was set in advance. What is the best response?

options.A: Reverse the decision rule: ship only if cost falls, regardless of quality.
options.B: Cancel the test, since A/B testing cannot be applied to language models.
options.C: Treat these results as exploratory. Set a primary metric, target sample size, and cost and latency guardrails before running a fresh confirmatory test.
options.D: Ship it, because quality improved and users prefer the new version.

explanation:
C is right because the team saw the results before choosing a metric or sample size. Use this run to plan a new test with a decision rule fixed before the team sees the results.
D fails because the difference is not established and cost rose notably.
B fails because A/B tests work for language model changes.
A fails because it ignores quality entirely.

question: A company wants every developer's Claude Code to deny access to production credentials files, permit only approved MCP servers, and send usage telemetry to a central collector. Developers can edit their own project and user settings. Which approach enforces the policy?

options.A: Publish the policy in the engineering handbook and ask developers to follow it.
options.B: Commit a settings file into each repository, which developers can edit locally.
options.C: Deploy managed settings with permission rules, an MCP allowlist and telemetry configuration, which take precedence and cannot be overridden by user or project settings.
options.D: Rely on each developer to write a personal instruction file that states the rules.

explanation:
C is right because organization policy must be enforced at a level users cannot override, and managed settings are designed for that.
A fails because documentation is not enforcement.
B fails because project settings can be changed or overridden by the developer.
D fails because personal instructions are voluntary and not a control.

question: A document-analysis product sees frequent 429 responses with retry-after headers during business hours. Dashboards show requests per minute are well below the account's request limit, but each request carries large documents and input tokens per minute are consistently at the ceiling. Which approach best reflects the real binding constraint?

options.A: Add a requests-per-minute limiter on the client at a lower value than the account limit.
options.B: Split each document into many tiny requests to stay below any per-request threshold.
options.C: Add a token-aware admission controller that paces work by estimated tokens, queues non-urgent requests or sends them to batch, and request additional capacity if demand is sustained.
options.D: Increase the number of retries on 429s so that the requests eventually go through.

explanation:
C is right because the constraint is token throughput, so admission has to be shaped by tokens, with deferrable work moved elsewhere.
A fails because the request rate is not the limiter, so capping it would reduce throughput without addressing token use.
D fails because retries add load to a saturated resource.
B fails because splitting increases overhead and repeated context, and total tokens still hit the limit.

question: Five teams in an organization use four different agent frameworks. Each has its own tracing, its own guardrails and its own eval scripts, so incidents are slow to diagnose and fixes are not shared. A platform lead must propose a standard. Which proposal is best?

options.A: Let every team keep its framework, because agent requirements differ too much to share anything.
options.B: Mandate whichever framework has the most community stars, and require all teams to migrate within a quarter.
options.C: Have each team build a custom harness from scratch, so that no external framework can constrain it.
options.D: Standardize on one agent harness and shared interfaces for tracing, evals and guardrails, plus a small catalog of reusable patterns, and let teams deviate with data showing a need.

explanation:
D is right because the cost today is fragmentation of operational tooling, and a standard harness with shared telemetry and patterns lets fixes and evals be reused while still allowing evidence-based exceptions.
A fails because it preserves the fragmentation that slows incident response.
B fails because popularity is not a selection criterion and a forced migration ignores existing eval and operational data.
C fails because custom harnesses multiply maintenance and reduce sharing further.

question: A retrieval-grounded assistant sometimes gives answers that cannot be traced to any source. The team wants telemetry that makes grounding and prompt changes traceable in production without logging user content. Which two additions help most? (Choose two.)

options.A: Record the document and chunk ids retrieved for each answer with their scores, and which of them were cited in the response.
options.B: Stamp every span with the prompt version and model identifier in use.
options.C: Capture the sampling temperature but no other attribute of the request.
options.D: Store full prompts and completions in the general analytics warehouse for all users.
options.E: Log only errors, since successful traces are not useful for grounding.

explanation:
A is right because source ids and citation links give grounding traceability using identifiers, not user text.
B is right because version and model tags let you tie a behavior change to a deployment.
D fails because it stores sensitive content broadly and violates the constraint.
E fails because ungrounded answers appear on successful requests.
C fails because temperature alone cannot explain provenance.

question: A team is measuring inter-rater reliability for a rubric where 95% of examples are acceptable and 5% are not. Which two practices are sound? (Choose two.)

options.A: Rely on percent agreement alone, because 95% agreement is automatically good.
options.B: Measure agreement among human annotators first, since it limits how well any judge can be expected to agree with them.
options.C: Use a single annotator, since a second annotator only adds cost.
options.D: Treat the judge's labels as truth when the humans disagree with them.
options.E: Use a chance-corrected statistic such as Cohen's kappa alongside percent agreement, because with imbalanced classes raw agreement can look high by chance.

explanation:
B is right because human agreement is the ceiling for the task and shows whether the rubric is clear.
E is right because kappa corrects for chance in a skewed class distribution.
A fails because a rater who always says acceptable already achieves 95%.
C fails because one annotator gives no reliability estimate.
D fails because it defeats the purpose of validating the judge.

question: Auditors ask how the team will reconstruct what an autonomous agent did on behalf of a user if a data incident occurs. Which audit design is best?

options.A: Log only failed requests, since successes are not security-relevant.
options.B: Keep the model's conversation transcripts, since they contain everything, keeping the current monitoring, keeping the current monitoring.
options.C: Write tamper-resistant logs of security-relevant actions, such as tool calls, parameters or hashes, approvals, denials and credential use, tied to an agent identity and the requesting user, without logging secrets.
options.D: Allow the agent to write its own summary of what it did after each run.

explanation:
C is right because accountability requires attributable, trustworthy records of actions and decisions, designed to avoid capturing secrets.
B fails because transcripts may lack authoritative records of actions and can hold sensitive content.
A fails because successful actions, such as data reads, are what an incident review needs.
D fails because a self-report can be wrong or manipulated.

question: During an outage in which answers are degraded for about 20% of users, the incident commander wants the response to be well organized. Which two actions are appropriate? (Choose two.)

options.A: Classify severity by user impact, choose the lowest-risk mitigation such as rollback, traffic shedding or a degraded path, and assign an owner.
options.B: Pause all other deployments for the rest of the quarter.
options.C: Send raw traces containing customer content to the affected customers as proof of the issue.
options.D: Delay all communication until the root cause is confirmed, so that updates are accurate.
options.E: Post status updates with the observed impact and a time for the next update, even before the cause is known.

explanation:
A is right because triage by impact and a reversible mitigation restore service quickly with clear ownership.
E is right because regular honest updates build trust while investigation continues.
D fails because silence leaves customers uninformed during impact.
C fails because sharing raw traces risks leaking other users' data.
B fails because a quarter-long freeze is disproportionate and does not address the cause.

question: Fleet telemetry from a 30-agent migration shows 40% of pull requests conflict, and nearly all conflicts involve the same shared configuration file that most subtasks touch. Which action best addresses this?

options.A: Revisit the decomposition: land the shared configuration change first in a dedicated step, or give one agent ownership of it, so that other subtasks do not edit it.
options.B: Ask the agents to resolve their conflicts by choosing the newest version of each file.
options.C: Stop collecting the telemetry, which only shows noise.
options.D: Increase the number of agents so that more work finishes before conflicts occur.

explanation:
A is right because the data points to overlapping ownership in the decomposition, which should be fixed at the design level.
D fails because more agents increase the number of conflicting edits.
B fails because newest-wins silently discards work and can break the build.
C fails because telemetry is what identified the systemic cause.

question: A team wants to roll out a new version of a production system prompt for a high-traffic assistant. Which two practices best reduce the risk? (Choose two.)

options.A: Keep prompts in a versioned registry referenced by configuration, so that rolling back is a configuration change and every response is traceable to a prompt version.
options.B: Release gradually through shadow or canary traffic, compare quality, refusal and cost metrics against the baseline, and roll back automatically on regression.
options.C: Ship to all traffic if the offline evaluation passes, since the offline suite already covers every case.
options.D: Schedule the release for the lowest-traffic hour so that fewer users are affected, without a rollback plan.
options.E: Edit the live prompt in place so that the change reaches all users immediately and any issue is seen quickly.

explanation:
A is right because versioned, configuration-driven prompts make change attributable and reversible.
B is right because a progressive rollout with guardrail metrics catches live regressions on a small slice.
E fails because in-place edits lose history and can hit everyone at once.
C fails because offline suites miss live distribution and need online confirmation.
D fails because a quiet hour reduces exposure only slightly and offers no way back.

question: A team deploys a remote MCP server that exposes internal HR tools. It currently uses one shared static bearer token stored in each employee's client configuration. The security team objects. Which design best fits MCP's authorization model?

options.A: Restrict the server to a local stdio process on each laptop and share the service credentials in the config.
options.B: Require OAuth-based authorization so that each user obtains a scoped access token, and have the server validate that tokens were issued for it and check the user's permissions per tool.
options.C: Keep the shared token and add a line in each tool description telling the model to only call tools for the logged-in user.
options.D: Keep the shared token but rotate it monthly and put it behind the corporate VPN.

explanation:
B is right because per-user, scoped, audience-checked tokens make actions attributable and limit what a stolen token can do.
D fails because a shared token still cannot identify users and a leaked one grants everything until rotation.
A fails because it spreads the service credentials to every laptop and does not authorize per user.
C fails because a tool description is a prompt, not an access control.

question: A remote MCP server receives a user's access token from the MCP client and forwards the same token to a downstream corporate API when a tool is called. A security review flags this as a vulnerability. Which remediation is correct?

options.A: Keep passing the token through but log every downstream call with the user id.
options.B: Encrypt the token in transit between the server and the downstream API and keep the design.
options.C: Do not pass the client's token through; have the server authenticate to the downstream API with its own credentials or a properly delegated token issued for that API, and enforce the user's permissions.
options.D: Pass the token through but only to APIs on the internal network.

explanation:
C is right because forwarding a token issued for one audience to another service breaks audience binding and creates confused-deputy risks, so the server should use credentials issued for the downstream API.
A fails because logging detects misuse rather than preventing it.
D fails because network location does not fix the token's wrong audience.
B fails because transport encryption protects the wire, not the design flaw.

question: An agent repeatedly calls a search tool, 25 times in one run, with slightly varied parameters. Traces show every call returns the same short text, 'Error: invalid request', and the loop stops only at the turn limit. What should the team change?

options.A: Remove the tool's error output so the model does not get distracted, keeping the current monitoring, keeping the current monitoring.
options.B: Increase the turn limit so that the agent has more attempts to find a working call.
options.C: Switch to a larger model so that it can guess the correct parameters.
options.D: Make the tool return specific, actionable, structured errors that say what was invalid and how to fix it, and add a loop guard that stops repeated identical failures.

explanation:
D is right because the harness and tool gave the model nothing to learn from and no brake, so improving the error contract and adding a guard addresses both.
B fails because more attempts with the same uninformative feedback burn more tokens.
C fails because guessing against an opaque error remains unreliable.
A fails because withholding error information removes the only signal the model has.

question: An agent loop that reads large documents begins to see responses with stop_reason model_context_window_exceeded. The team's fallback logic retries failed calls on a second model and the same stop appears there too, doubling cost. What should the loop do on this stop reason?

options.A: Raise max_tokens so that the response can complete within the window.
options.B: Back off and retry the identical request, because the condition is a transient capacity issue.
options.C: Treat the output as truncated and reduce the context, for example by editing out stale tool results or compacting, then continue, instead of retrying elsewhere.
options.D: Route the request to the safety-handling path, because the model declined to continue.

explanation:
C is right because the response filled the model's context window; the input and output together do not fit, so the fix is to shrink what is in context and continue.
B fails because the condition is deterministic for that input, not transient.
D fails because this is not a refusal; a refusal has its own stop reason.
A fails because raising the output allowance cannot create room in a window that is already full.

question: A team uses a model alias that the provider moved to a newer snapshot. Within a day, the refusal rate rose from 0.5% to 3% and the answer style changed, but nothing in the team's own deployment changed. Which practice would have made this both preventable and quickly diagnosable?

options.A: Switch to a model from a different provider with every release to avoid dependency.
options.B: Pin an explicit model snapshot, record the model identifier on every response, and roll upgrades through a canary comparison against the baseline.
options.C: Add a system prompt instruction asking the model to refuse less often.
options.D: Disable alerting on refusal rate, since the rate is expected to fluctuate.

explanation:
B is right because pinning removes silent behavior changes, the identifier makes cohorts comparable, and a canary reveals drift on a small slice first.
C fails because a prompt patch leaves the cause unaddressed and may mask a real policy behavior.
A fails because it multiplies migration work.
D fails because it removes the signal that detected the problem.

question: A coding agent has shell access in a developer environment. It once ran a command that dropped a table in a shared staging database. The team's system prompt already says 'never run destructive commands'. Which control best prevents a recurrence?

options.A: Log every shell command so that the team can restore the table later.
options.B: Repeat the instruction in capital letters near the top of the system prompt.
options.C: Reduce the agent's effort level, so that it is less likely to run risky commands.
options.D: A pre-tool-use hook or permission rule that denies destructive commands and requests against shared databases, enforced outside the model, with human approval for exceptions.

explanation:
D is right because a deterministic check runs before the action and does not depend on the model complying.
B fails because emphasis does not make an instruction enforceable.
A fails because logging helps recovery, not prevention.

question: Monthly cost for an assistant doubled with no growth in traffic. The team has dashboards for request counts and total tokens, but cannot see why. The application relies on prompt caching. Which telemetry addition would most quickly reveal the cause?

options.A: Track average response length in characters by hour.
options.B: Record cache read and cache creation token counts on every request, together with a hash of the prompt prefix, and compare them across requests.
options.C: Add a counter of HTTP 200 responses by endpoint.
options.D: Log the full text of every prompt so that engineers can read them.

explanation:
B is right because cache reads, cache writes and prefix hashes show whether the stable prefix is actually matching, and a prefix that changes between requests, for example because of an embedded timestamp, shows up as constant cache creation and no reads.
C fails because success counts say nothing about token mix.
D fails because reading prompts by hand is slow and a privacy risk, and it does not quantify cache behavior.
A fails because output length affects cost but would not explain a doubling with caching in play.

question: A team needs a merge and conflict strategy for parallel agents working on a large service. Which two practices are most effective? (Choose two.)

options.A: Assign disjoint file or module ownership and define interfaces between parts up front, so that parallel work rarely overlaps.
options.B: Merge in a planned order and run the full test suite after each integration, to catch cross-branch breakage early.
options.C: Let each agent rebase onto whichever other agent's branch finished last.
options.D: Have every agent attempt the whole task independently and merge the majority result.
options.E: Merge any branch automatically as soon as its own tests pass, regardless of the other branches.

explanation:
A is right because clear boundaries reduce conflicts at the source.
B is right because branches that pass alone can still break when combined, so integration testing is needed.
E fails because per-branch tests do not cover interactions.
C fails because ad hoc rebasing creates tangled dependencies.
D fails because redundant attempts multiply cost and merging them produces conflicts.

question: A scheduled agent runs nightly for several hours to upgrade dependencies across repositories. Which two operational controls are most important? (Choose two.)

options.A: Remove all limits so that long runs always finish.
options.B: Give it administrator credentials so that it is never blocked by permissions.
options.C: Checkpoint progress so that an interrupted run resumes where it stopped, and set turn and budget limits.
options.D: Define notification and escalation, so that the agent stops and alerts an owner when it is blocked or reaches a risky step instead of improvising.
options.E: Notify humans only when a run succeeds, since failures are expected.

explanation:
C is right because durability and bounds keep a long unattended run recoverable and affordable.
D is right because escalation turns a blocked or risky situation into a human decision.
B fails because broad credentials turn a mistake into damage.
E fails because silence on failures hides problems.
A fails because unbounded runs can loop and spend without control.
